power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: We used terms related to low back pain, digital health technologies, and randomised trials, and screened the reference lists of systematic reviews.
Previous reviews examined individual modalities, such as mobile applications, telehealth, or virtual reality, and used pairwise meta-analysis.
Existing network meta-analyses either included broader chronic pain populations or compared a narrower range of rehabilitation approaches for low back pain.
Although these reviews suggested that some digital interventions might improve pain or physical function, their relative effects across clinical outcomes and follow-up periods remained uncertain.

To our knowledge, no previous synthesis had compared digital delivery modalities for low back pain across pain, physical function, and psychosocial outcomes while assessing confidence in the network estimates.
This systematic review and network meta-analysis included 92 reports from 84 randomised controlled trials involving 11 803 participants.

We compared six digital modalities-telemedicine, web applications, mobile applications, virtual reality, exergaming, and biofeedback devices-with face-to-face care and control across seven outcomes and follow-up periods extending from treatment completion to 12 months or longer.

Virtual reality had the broadest favourable estimates at post-intervention, including reductions in pain intensity and pain-related fear avoidance and improvement in health-related quality of life, all supported by moderate-confidence evidence.
Other modalities showed favourable effects for selected outcomes, but no stable hierarchy was observed across outcomes and follow-up periods.
Confidence in many estimates was low or very low, the post-intervention pain-intensity network showed inconsistency, and longer-term networks were sparse.
These findings distinguish favourable post-intervention estimates from evidence of sustained comparative superiority.
Digital health interventions might support the management of low back pain, but the available evidence does not establish that any single delivery modality should be preferred.

Although virtual reality produced the broadest favourable post-intervention estimates, evidence of sustained superiority was not established, and the observed effects cannot be separated reliably from differences in therapeutic content, treatment intensity, and clinician support.
Selection of a digital intervention should therefore consider the intended treatment outcome, therapeutic components, accessibility, digital literacy, costs, and patient preferences.

Adequately powered head-to-head trials with longer follow-up are needed, together with component-based studies that distinguish the contribution of the technological platform from that of the treatment it delivers.

Digital health interventions are increasingly used for low back pain, but their comparative effectiveness across different delivery modalities, clinical outcomes, and follow-up periods remains uncertain.
We aimed to compare the effects of major digital health modalities for adults with low back pain.
We conducted a systematic review and frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, APA PsycINFO, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP were searched from inception to March 19, 2026, and updated to Aug 8, 2026.
Eight treatment nodes were compared: telemedicine, web applications, mobile applications, virtual reality, exergaming, biofeedback devices, face-to-face care, and control.
Primary outcomes were pain intensity and physical function; secondary outcomes were pain-related fear avoidance, health-related quality of life, self-efficacy, anxiety, and depression.
The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261339841).
We included 92 reports from 84 randomised controlled trials involving 11 803 participants.
At post-intervention, virtual reality had the most favourable point estimate for pain intensity (SMD -1.43, 95% CI -1.87 to -0.98; moderate confidence).
The estimate for physical function also favoured virtual reality (-0.86, -1.45 to -0.26), although confidence was very low.
Virtual reality also probably reduced pain-related fear avoidance (-1.14, -1.68 to -0.61) and improved health-related quality of life (0.97, 0.57 to 1.36), both with moderate confidence.
Other digital modalities showed favourable effects for selected outcomes, but confidence was generally low or very low.
Networks became progressively sparse at later follow-up, and sustained effects were inconsistent.
Global inconsistency was detected in the post-intervention pain-intensity network, with local inconsistency for selected exergaming comparisons.
Digital health interventions for low back pain showed different effects across outcomes and follow-up periods.

Virtual reality had the most favourable post-intervention estimates for pain intensity, pain-related fear avoidance, and health-related quality of life compared with control, with moderate confidence in these estimates.
Larger head-to-head trials with longer follow-up are needed to determine whether these effects are sustained and to clarify the comparative effectiveness of digital interventions.

Low back pain is commonly defined as pain between the lower costal margin and the gluteal folds, with or without leg pain. 1 In 2020, it affected approximately 619 million people worldwide and remains the leading cause of years lived with disability, imposing a substantial burden through pain, functional limitation, and psychological distress. 2, 3 Healthcare spending on low back and neck pain in the United States was estimated at US$134.5 billion in 2016. 4 Management of low back pain includes both pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments. 5 However, pharmacological therapies generally provide only small, predominantly short-term benefits and may increase adverse events. 6 Therefore, non-pharmacological strategies are central to guideline-based management, including education and supported self-management, exercise, psychological therapies, and multidisciplinary care. 5, 7 Digital health encompasses the use of digital technologies to support health and healthcare delivery. 8, 9 In low back pain, these technologies include telemedicine and telerehabilitation, web and mobile applications, virtual reality, exergaming, and biofeedback devices.

text.text: Digital health interventions can deliver education, exercise, self-management support, monitoring, and interactive rehabilitation, and may complement conventional care. 10, 11 Previous systematic reviews only evaluated mobile applications, telerehabilitation, or virtual reality separately, using conventional pairwise meta-analyses. [12] [13] [14] [15] At the network level, a recent analysis of chronic non-specific low back pain compared AI-assisted telerehabilitation, telerehabilitation, in-person rehabilitation, and usual care, but did not incorporate the broader range of digital modalities available for low back pain. 16 Consequently, the comparative effectiveness of these modalities for specific clinical outcomes and follow-up periods remains uncertain, limiting evidence-based treatment selection and implementation.

text.text: To address this evidence gap, we conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials evaluating digital health interventions for adults with low back pain.
Unlike conventional pairwise meta-analysis, network meta-analysis combines direct and indirect evidence to enable simultaneous comparison of multiple interventions.
We compared eight treatment nodes, including telemedicine, web applications, mobile applications, virtual reality, exergaming, biofeedback devices, face-to-face care, and control.
Their effects on pain intensity, physical function, and other clinical outcomes were evaluated from post-intervention to 12 months or longer.
This comprehensive comparative framework aims to provide clinically relevant evidence to inform treatment selection and future guideline recommendations for digital health in low back pain care.

This systematic review and network meta-analysis was reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement and the PRISMA extension for network meta-analyses. 17, 18 Completed reporting checklists are provided in the appendix (pp 6-12).

text.text: The protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO before study selection and data extraction began (CRD420261339841), and deviations from the registered protocol are described in the appendix (p 13).

We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), CINAHL, APA PsycINFO, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) from inception to 19 March 2026, with an updated search to 8 August 2026.
Reference lists of relevant systematic reviews were also screened.
Full search strategies are provided in appendix (pp 14-33).
We included randomised controlled trials evaluating digital health interventions in adults aged 18 years or older with low back pain.

Treatment nodes were defined before data synthesis according to the principal mode of digital delivery, informed by previous systematic reviews and network meta-analyses. [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] Eight nodes were defined: control, face-to-face care, telemedicine, web applications (Web-App), mobile applications (Mobile-App), biofeedback devices, virtual reality (VR), and exergaming.

text.text: Waiting-list, no-intervention, background usual care without study-specific active treatment, minimal advice or education, and sham or attention controls were classified as control; structured in-person physiotherapy or exercise programmes were classified as face-to-face care.
Detailed operational definitions, boundary rules, and classifications of individual study arms are provided in appendix (pp 54-69).
Paired reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, trial registry records where applicable, and potentially eligible full-text reports.
Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with another reviewer.
Multiple reports or registry records from the same trial were linked and treated as a single study.

The most complete published report was designated as the primary report, with companion reports and registry records used to supplement study characteristics, risk-of-bias assessments, and outcome data.
Data were extracted independently by paired reviewers using a standardised form.
Extracted information included study and participant characteristics, intervention characteristics, and outcomes; detailed study characteristics are provided in appendix (pp 70-78).
Discrepancies were resolved by discussion.

We assessed two primary outcomes, pain intensity and physical function, and five secondary outcomes, pain-related fear avoidance, health-related quality of life, self-efficacy, anxiety, and depression, all analysed as continuous outcomes. [24] [25] [26] [27] Outcome data were extracted at all available follow-up assessments and classified according to time since completion of the intervention as post-intervention (end of treatment or <2 months), short-term (≥2 to <6 months), mid-term (≥6 to <12 months), and long-term (≥12 months). 27 Post-intervention was the primary time point for effectiveness analyses.

When multiple instruments assessed the same outcome, one measure was selected according to the prespecified hierarchy described in appendix (pp 79-84).

Risk of bias was assessed independently by paired reviewers using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2). 28, 29 Overall judgments were classified as low risk of bias, some concerns, or high risk of bias.

Because outcomes were measured using different instruments, effects were expressed as standardised mean differences (SMDs; Hedges' g) with 95% CIs.

Scale directions were harmonised so that negative SMDs indicated improvement in pain intensity, physical function, pain-related fear avoidance, anxiety, and depression, and positive SMDs indicated improvement in health-related quality of life and self-efficacy.
Endpoint scores were used at each follow-up.

Missing or incomplete data were sought from investigators or derived or converted using established methods. 30, 31 Separate frequentist random-effects network meta-analyses were conducted for each outcome and follow-up interval with a connected network, using the graph-theoretical approach in netmeta. 32, 33 Between-study variance was estimated by restricted maximum likelihood and assumed common across treatment comparisons within each network.

Control was the reference treatment.

An absolute SMD of 0.50 was used as a pragmatic threshold for potential clinical importance, consistent with a previous network meta-analysis of low back pain interventions. 27 This threshold aided interpretation across outcomes but was not a validated outcome-specific minimal important difference.

Two sensitivity analyses were conducted for connected networks: excluding studies at overall high risk of bias and excluding studies with outcome data that were statistically estimated, converted, or otherwise derived rather than directly reported (appendix pp 141-165).
Robustness was assessed by comparing the direction, magnitude, and 95% CIs of network estimates with those from the primary analyses.

As a modification of the registered subgroup analysis by low back pain duration, we also conducted a restricted analysis including only trials enrolling participants with chronic low back pain, defined as symptoms lasting at least 12 weeks (appendix pp 166-178).

Because this analysis did not formally compare treatment effects between chronic and non-chronic populations, it was interpreted as a restricted-population analysis rather than evidence of effect modification.

Confidence in all post-intervention network estimates and in short-term estimates for pain intensity and physical function was assessed using the CINeMA framework. 38, 39 Overall confidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low across six domains: within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, and incoherence.

Beyond post-intervention, networks became progressively sparser, and favourable estimates were less consistent across outcomes and follow-up periods.

At post-intervention, VR probably reduced pain intensity compared with control (SMD -1.43, 95% CI -1.87 to -0.98; moderate confidence).

Estimates also favoured lower pain intensity with exergaming (-1.09, -1.73 to -0.44), Mobile-App (-0.67, -1.08 to -0.26), Web-App (-0.54, -1.06 to -0.02), and telemedicine (-0.51, -0.94 to -0.07), but confidence in the evidence was very low.
Estimates for the remaining interventions were uncertain.

For post-intervention physical function, estimates favoured better physical function for VR (SMD -0.86, 95% CI -1.45 to -0.26), Web-App (-0.78, -1.27 to -0.30), Mobile-App (-0.73, -1.22 to -0.23), biofeedback devices (-0.70, -1.38 to -0.03), and telemedicine (-0.57, -1.01 to -0.13), but confidence in the evidence was very low.

For health-related quality of life, VR probably improved health-related quality of life compared with control (SMD 0.97, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.36; moderate confidence).
Estimates also favoured Mobile-App (0.44, 0.15 to 0.74), telemedicine (0.43, 0.15 to 0.72), and face-to-face care (0.35, 0.03 to 0.67), although confidence in the evidence was very low.

For self-efficacy, Exergaming favoured better self-efficacy (SMD 0.77, 95% CI 0.05 to 1.49), whereas the estimate for Mobile-App (0.48, 0.00 to 0.97) included the null; confidence was very low for both comparisons.

text.text: Sensitivity analyses excluding studies at high overall risk of bias and those with statistically estimated or converted outcome data were conducted across connected outcome networks.

The direction of estimates was generally similar to that in the primary analyses, although exclusion of studies reduced network connectivity and precision for several sparse secondary-outcome networks (appendix pp 141-165).

In restricted-population analyses including only participants with chronic low back pain, the direction of post-intervention treatment effects was generally consistent with the primary analyses, although some estimates were less precise (appendix pp 166-178).

In this systematic review and network meta-analysis of 84 randomised controlled trials involving 11 803 participants, the comparative effects of digital health interventions varied across outcomes and follow-up periods.

At post-intervention, compared with control, VR showed the most favourable estimates across pain intensity, physical function, pain-related fear avoidance, and health-related quality of life, with moderate confidence for pain intensity, pain-related fear avoidance, and health-related quality of life, but very low confidence for physical function.

Other digital modalities showed favourable estimates in a narrower range of outcomes: Mobile-App and telemedicine favoured lower pain intensity, better physical function, and better health-related quality of life; Web-App and biofeedback devices mainly favoured better physical function; and exergaming favoured lower pain intensity.
Beyond post-intervention, favourable estimates were less consistent across outcomes and follow-up periods.
Longer-term networks were increasingly sparse, and most mid-term and long-term estimates were not formally assessed with CINeMA, precluding conclusions about sustained comparative superiority.
Several features may help explain the modality-specific patterns observed in our analysis.

VR combines immersive experience with therapeutic strategies such as distraction, pain education, behavioural skills training, and movement-based rehabilitation. 11, 40, 41 These features may reduce attention to pain and threat and facilitate graded exposure, potentially contributing to the favourable post-intervention estimates for pain intensity and pain-related fear avoidance, although the independent contribution of immersion remains uncertain.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that modality-level differences should be interpreted in the context of the therapeutic content delivered, rather than attributed to the technological platform alone.
Our findings are broadly consistent with previous evidence on digital interventions for low back pain.

A meta-analysis of VR-based training reported improvements in pain, pain-related fear avoidance, and disability immediately after treatment, whereas effects at 3-6 months remained inconclusive. 15 Reviews of mobile health, mobile apps, and telehealth have reported mixed findings for pain and disability, with benefits varying across interventions and assessment periods. [12] [13] [14] Previous syntheses have evaluated digital interventions across broader populations with chronic or musculoskeletal pain, 20, 21 whereas a recent network meta-analysis focused on low back pain but compared only AI-assisted telerehabilitation, conventional telerehabilitation, in-person care, and usual care. 16 Our study extends this evidence by comparing six digital modalities across seven clinical outcomes and multiple follow-up periods.

text.text: Although VR showed favourable estimates across several outcomes at post-intervention, these findings do not establish its sustained superiority over other modalities.
Limited direct comparisons, sparse longer-term networks, and predominantly low or very low confidence in the evidence constrain comparative treatment recommendations.

Current guidelines recommend education, exercise, psychological therapies, and supported self-management as core components of non-pharmacological care for low back pain, 45, 46 while WHO guidance emphasises a person-centred, multimodal approach. 47 However, guidance on selecting digital modalities to deliver these interventions remains limited.

text.text: We used a modality-based classification and systematically assessed transitivity, heterogeneity, inconsistency, and confidence in network estimates using CINeMA.
Several limitations arose from the primary trials.

First, study populations were clinically heterogeneous in terms of pain duration (acute, subacute, chronic, or mixed) and clinical classification, which may have contributed to variation in treatment effects.

Second, comparator conditions varied substantially, ranging from waiting-list or minimal-care controls to usual care and structured face-to-face rehabilitation, which may have influenced relative effect estimates.
Third, many trials raised risk-of-bias concerns.
Blinding was often infeasible, while missing data, selective reporting, and deviations from intended interventions further reduced confidence in the evidence.
These limitations were partly mitigated by rigorous risk-of-bias assessment, sensitivity analyses, and evaluation of transitivity, inconsistency, and confidence in the evidence.

Fourth, evidence on adverse events, acceptability, treatment discontinuation, and treatment burden was limited or not synthesised, preventing a complete assessment of the balance between benefit and burden.
Several limitations also arose from the network meta-analysis itself.

First, substantial heterogeneity was present in several networks, and global inconsistency was detected in the post-intervention pain-intensity network, with local disagreement for selected exergaming comparisons; these findings warrant cautious interpretation.
Second, direct comparisons between digital modalities were limited, and networks became increasingly sparse at longer follow-up, reducing the precision of long-term estimates.

Third, analyses relied on aggregate study-level data, and interventions within each modality node varied in therapeutic content, intensity, duration, and clinician support, limiting our ability to explore treatment-effect modifiers and disentangle the effects of the technological platform from those of specific therapeutic components.
Fourth, although SMDs allowed outcomes measured with different instruments to be combined, they are less intuitive clinically.

Back-transformed estimates for pain intensity and physical function depended on the selected reference standard deviations and should not be interpreted as instrument-specific minimally important differences.
Future research on digital health for low back pain should focus on four priorities.
First, adequately powered head-to-head trials with longer follow-up are needed.
Second, factorial or component-based studies should distinguish the effects of therapeutic content, clinician support, treatment intensity, and technological features.

Third, broader outcomes beyond pain and function, including anxiety, depression, sleep, and long-term improvement, should be evaluated in people with low back pain. 53 These outcomes are clinically relevant because low back pain is often accompanied by psychological and behavioural comorbidities that may also be influenced by digital interventions.
text.formatted: Third, broader outcomes beyond pain and function, including anxiety, depression, sleep, and long-term improvement, should be evaluated in people with low back pain. <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> These outcomes are clinically relevant because low back pain is often accompanied by psychological and behavioural comorbidities that may also be influenced by digital interventions.

text.text: Finally, pragmatic studies should assess cost-effectiveness, accessibility, digital exclusion, and implementation in routine care.
Digital health interventions for low back pain showed effects that varied across outcomes and follow-up periods.

Virtual reality had the most favourable post-intervention estimates, with moderate-confidence evidence for improvements in pain intensity, pain-related fear avoidance, and health-related quality of life.

Although longer-term effects and the relative benefits of different modalities remain uncertain, these findings highlight the potential of digital interventions for low back pain management and the need for adequately powered head-to-head trials with longer follow-up.
